stem.en: The maximum number of members in a private company is:

explanation.en: Under Section 2(68) of the Companies Act, 2013, a private company can have at most 200 members (excluding certain employees).

stem.en: Preference shares carry a preferential right in respect of:

options.en: Dividend and repayment of capital on winding up

explanation.en: Preference shareholders are paid a fixed dividend and get their capital back before equity shareholders on winding up.

stem.en: Reserve capital is:

options.en: The part of uncalled capital that will be called up only on winding up
Capital kept in a reserve fund

explanation.en: By special resolution, a company may decide that part of its uncalled capital will be called only on winding up.

stem.en: 50,000 shares of ₹10 each are subscribed and ₹7 per share is called up. Calls in arrears are ₹3,000. Paid-up capital is:
As per Table F of the Companies Act, 2013, interest on calls in arrears may be charged at a rate not exceeding:

explanation.en: Table F allows up to 10% p.a. on calls in arrears (and up to 12% p.a. on calls in advance).

stem.en: Calls in advance are shown in the balance sheet under:

explanation.en: Calls in advance are money owed back (or adjusted later) to shareholders and are shown under other current liabilities.

stem.en: 20,000 shares of ₹10 are issued at par: ₹2 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹5 on call. A holder of 500 shares paid only the application money. Total cash received by the company is:
The balance of Calls in Arrears Account is shown:

options.en: As a deduction from called-up capital in the notes to accounts

explanation.en: Called-up capital less calls in arrears gives the paid-up capital.

stem.en: A company buys assets for ₹3,60,000 and pays by issuing shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2. The number of shares issued is:

explanation.en: Issue price = ₹12; 3,60,000 ÷ 12 = 30,000 shares.

stem.en: Securities premium CANNOT be used for:

options.en: Providing premium on redemption of debentures

explanation.en: Section 52 lists the permitted uses; payment of dividend is not one of them.

stem.en: Under the Companies Act, 2013, issue of shares at a discount is:

options.en: Not permitted, except sweat equity shares
Permitted with SEBI approval for any shares
Permitted up to 10% of face value

explanation.en: Section 53 prohibits issue at a discount; sweat equity shares (Section 54) are the exception.

stem.en: 10,000 shares of ₹10 are issued at a premium of ₹2, payable ₹3 on application, ₹5 (including premium) on allotment and ₹4 on call. The amount credited to Share Capital Account on allotment is:

explanation.en: Of ₹5 on allotment, ₹2 is premium and ₹3 is capital: 10,000 × 3 = ₹30,000.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): Premium received on issue of shares is credited to Securities Premium Account and not to Share Capital Account.
Reason (R): Share Capital Account is credited only with the face (nominal) value of shares.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Because share capital shows only the face value, the excess goes to Securities Premium; R explains A.

stem.en: A company offers 80,000 shares and receives applications for 1,20,000 shares. If all applicants get shares pro-rata, the pro-rata ratio is:
In pro-rata allotment, excess application money that cannot be adjusted towards allotment or calls is:

explanation.en: Any balance that cannot be adjusted is returned to the applicant.

stem.en: Shares of ₹10: ₹3 on application and ₹4 on allotment; allotment is pro-rata 2:3 and excess application money is adjusted on allotment. Ravi applied for 600 shares. The amount Ravi pays on allotment is:

explanation.en: Allotted = 600 × 2/3 = 400. Paid on application 1,800; needed 1,200; excess 600. Allotment due 1,600 − 600 = ₹1,000.

stem.en: Applications for 3,000 shares are rejected outright. Application money is ₹2 per share. The amount refunded to them is:

explanation.en: Rejected applicants get their full application money back: 3,000 × 2 = ₹6,000.

solution.en: Rejected applicants get their full application money back: 3,000 × 2 = ₹6,000.

stem.en: 200 shares of ₹10 each are forfeited for non-payment of the final call of ₹2 per share. The amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account is:

explanation.en: Amount received = 200 × (10 − 2) = ₹1,600.

stem.en: The maximum discount allowed on reissue of forfeited shares is:

options.en: The amount forfeited on those shares
The securities premium on those shares

explanation.en: The discount on reissue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares.

stem.en: 300 shares of ₹10 issued at a premium of ₹2 are forfeited: the holder paid ₹3 on application but not ₹5 on allotment (including premium) or ₹4 on call. The shares are reissued at ₹9 per share fully paid. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:

explanation.en: Forfeited amount = 300 × 3 = 900 (premium unpaid, so it is cancelled). Discount on reissue = 300 × 1 = 300. Capital reserve = 900 − 300 = ₹600.

stem.en: After reissue of forfeited shares, the balance of Share Forfeiture Account relating to those shares is transferred to:

explanation.en: The gain is a capital profit and goes to Capital Reserve.

stem.en: How many shares were allotted to Mohan?

passage.en: Vidya Ltd invited applications for 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable ₹3 on application, ₹5 (including premium) on allotment and ₹4 on first and final call. Applications were received for 30,000 shares and allotment was made pro-rata to all applicants. Excess application money was adjusted towards allotment. Mohan, who had applied for 300 shares, failed to pay the allotment and call money.

stem.en: How much allotment money (after adjusting his excess application money) remained unpaid by Mohan?

passage.en: Vidya Ltd invited applications for 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, payable ₹3 on application, ₹5 (including premium) on allotment and ₹4 on first and final call. Applications were received for 30,000 shares and allotment was made pro-rata to all applicants. Excess application money was adjusted towards allotment. Mohan, who had applied for 300 shares, failed to pay the allotment and call money.

explanation.en: Mohan paid 300 × 3 = 900 on application; needed 200 × 3 = 600; excess 300. Allotment due 200 × 5 = 1,000, so ₹700 remained unpaid.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): The balance in Share Forfeiture Account after reissue of forfeited shares is transferred to Capital Reserve.
Reason (R): The gain on forfeited shares is a capital profit and not a revenue profit.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Being a capital profit, it cannot be distributed as dividend and is taken to Capital Reserve; R explains A.

stem.en: A company issued 20,000 shares of ₹10 each payable ₹4 on application, ₹3 on allotment and ₹3 on call. Applications were received for 30,000 shares and shares were allotted pro-rata; excess application money was adjusted on allotment. Ram, who applied for 600 shares, failed to pay the allotment money and his shares were forfeited before the call. The amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account is:

explanation.en: Ram is allotted 600 × 20,000/30,000 = 400 shares. He paid 600 × 4 = ₹2,400: ₹1,600 for application and ₹800 adjusted on allotment. All ₹2,400 received is forfeited (allotment unpaid = 400 × 3 − 800 = ₹400).

solution.en: He paid 600 × 4 = ₹2,400: ₹1,600 for application and ₹800 adjusted on allotment.

stem.en: 500 shares of ₹10 each, on which ₹6 per share had been paid, were forfeited. Of these, 300 shares were reissued at ₹8 per share as fully paid. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:

explanation.en: Forfeited on the 300 reissued shares = 300 × 6 = ₹1,800. Discount on reissue = 300 × 2 = ₹600. Capital reserve = 1,800 − 600 = ₹1,200.

stem.en: Under Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Securities Premium Account cannot be used for:

options.en: Writing off discount on issue of debentures

explanation.en: Securities premium may be used only for the purposes listed in Section 52 (bonus shares, preliminary expenses, expenses/discount on issue, premium on redemption, buy-back). It cannot be used to pay dividends.
